title: PPF Installation FAQ
subtitle: Common questions about installing PPF, the faults that show up, and how to fix them.
source: simonsays.coach — grounded in the Training Handbook, with external sources cited where relevant.

faqs.q: Why does PPF lift at the edges a few days after a clean-looking install?
faqs.a: Almost always surface prep. PPF is held on by molecular (Van der Waals) attraction, which only works when the adhesive and the paint touch within about a nanometre. A panel that looks clean to the eye can still carry wax, polish residue, silicone or fingerprints that hold the adhesive just far enough off the paint that it never fully bonds — so the edge lets go within days. Water and slip solution do not remove oils; the last wipe before film must be a degreaser (IPA or panel prep). If an edge peels back with no wrinkling, the bond never formed — re-prep and re-install rather than just re-heating.

handoutRefs.title: Van der Waals Adhesion — Why Surface Prep Matters

faqs.q: Do I really need to clay and IPA-wipe a brand-new car?
faqs.a: Yes. New paint looks clean but is almost always contaminated from transport, dealer prep and storage, and dealers often add a wax sealant that has to come off completely. Iron remover and clay are non-negotiable even on a car delivered yesterday, and the final IPA / panel-prep wipe is the last thing that touches the paint before the film. Skipping clay is the single most common prep shortcut and the one that produces the most long-term failures.

faqs.q: Can the final wipe before film be slip solution or water instead of a degreaser?
faqs.a: No. Slip solution and plain water do not remove oils — they just move them around. The last pass before the film must be a dedicated degreaser (IPA-based panel wipe or the film maker's prep solution), applied in straight overlapping passes until the cloth comes off the panel clean. Use lint-free, low-shed wipes; cheap microfibres leave fibres that end up trapped under the film.

faqs.q: An edge lifted within 24 hours on a curve. What does that tell me?
faqs.a: Lifting that shows up within the first day points to stretch or tack — not prep. On a curve or relief cut it is usually over-stretch: the film was pulled past its memory limit and is contracting back. Re-lift the section, let the film relax, re-position with less stretch, and post-heat to set it. The rule is to stretch only what the panel demands, never extra 'just in case'.

faqs.q: How do I stop edges lifting at wheel-arch lips and bumper corners?
faqs.a: Those are the highest-stretch zones, so they live or die on the post-heat. Stretch the film into the curve in small sections rather than bridging across it, use small relief cuts hidden in panel gaps where tension can't be relieved by stretch alone, then post-heat every wrapped edge and hold it down until it cools so the bond sets in position. Without that heat the stretch is only temporary and the memory pulls the edge back within days or weeks.

handoutRefs.title: SOP — Post-Heating: Surface Temperature and Technique

sources.label: Why PPF edges lift and how to prevent it (platinumplus)

faqs.q: My wrap looked perfect at the end of the job, then lifted two weeks later. Why?
faqs.a: The adhesive bond was probably fine — the stretch was not set. Stretched film has elastic memory: without heat to lock the polymer in its new shape it slowly tries to return, pulling at edges and corners. That's why a panel can look flawless on the day and fail later. Heat is what turns a temporary stretch into a permanent shape: no post-heat on stretched zones means no permanent install.

faqs.q: What surface temperature should I post-heat to?
faqs.a: Bring the film surface to 80–90 °C, measured at the film with an IR thermometer — not the heat-gun's dial. Below about 70 °C the adhesive won't flow into the clear coat and the film won't give up its memory; sustained much above 90 °C (or brief spikes beyond about 100 °C) risks distorting the film and damaging the clear coat. The 50–60 °C figure some people quote is the self-healing temperature, which is a different thing. The air leaving the gun can be 200 °C or more, so distance and dwell — not the dial — decide what the surface actually sees. Post-heat edges, recesses and curves only; the flat field doesn't need it.

handoutRefs.title: SOP — Post-Heating: Surface Temperature and Technique

faqs.q: How much should I stretch the film?
faqs.a: Only as much as the panel actually demands — extra stretch 'to be safe' just stores up memory pull-back later. Work the tension wet, at the panel: anchor the piece with tack, lift the working zone, pull the stretch the curve needs, then lay it down. While the film floats on slip you can add, release and redistribute tension freely; shaping the film in the air before lay-down is vinyl technique, not PPF. Squeegee outward from the most-stretched zone toward the edges, and set every stretched area with heat. If a corner won't lay flat the problem is usually upstream tension, not the corner itself.

faqs.q: What causes stretch marks — cloudy, whitened patches in the film?
faqs.a: Cold film stretched too aggressively over a tight radius. The fix is to reduce how much you stretch in one go and, if the film needs it, relax it with hot demineralised water or steam before stretching — work a 10 cm section at a time: relax if needed, stretch, lay down, post-heat with a heat gun, then move on. In a cold shop, bring the film and panel up to temperature before you start so the film isn't brittle.

faqs.q: How do I tell a water bubble from an air bubble?
faqs.a: Watch whether it shrinks. Water shows as a fine misty haze or a soft pocket that gets smaller day by day and clears on its own — water dissolves into the film and breathes out as vapour. Air is a discrete, domed pocket that does not shrink at all; it has no way out on its own and has to be worked out by hand on the day. A speck or ring at the centre of a pocket is trapped contamination, which won't clear by squeegee and means lifting and re-cleaning.

handoutRefs.title: Water Goes, Air Stays — The Science of Bubbles Under Fresh PPF

faqs.q: An air pocket won't clear. How do I remove it?
faqs.a: Air has no self-clearing route, so it's a mechanical job done on the day while the film is still movable. Work it to the nearest edge with firm, overlapping squeegee strokes — the shortest way out is the perimeter — then add heat and re-press so the film softens and the pocket flattens. Don't 'wait and see' on air the way you would with water: leave it and it's still there next week, only now the adhesive has set and it's far harder to move.

faqs.q: Should I pin-prick a bubble to release it?
faqs.a: Only as a last resort, on the day, for a small stubborn air pocket that won't move to an edge — a single fine prick at the edge of the bubble with a clean needle, followed by a press. Never pop water bubbles (they clear themselves) and never let a customer do it: a needle hole left in cured film is a permanent visible defect that can let in dirt and moisture.

faqs.q: What's the difference between slip and tack solution, and how do I mix them?
faqs.a: Slip solution is water plus a tiny amount of surfactant (purpose-made slip, or a few drops of baby shampoo per litre) — it lowers surface tension so you can position the film before the adhesive grabs. Tack solution is water plus roughly 10–25% isopropyl alcohol — used at edges and detail areas to displace the slip and bring the adhesive forward so it bonds. Mix both by ratio to the film maker's spec, not by feel: too much surfactant leaves edges that never fully bond, and solutions mixed by eye are the leading cause of inconsistent installs across staff.

handoutRefs.title: PPF Adhesives — How They Work and How They Fail

faqs.q: I'm working in a cold shop and the film barely tacks. What's wrong?
faqs.a: Cold slows tack development and makes the adhesive sluggish, so the film looks fine on day one and starts curling at the edges within a week or two. Don't install below the film maker's stated minimum panel temperature; aim for shop and panel temperatures around 20–25 °C, and warm both the panel and your solutions before starting in winter. Cold solutions straight from the tap effectively extend your working window but leave the customer with a film that's barely bonded at the edges.

faqs.q: How long does the adhesive take to cure, and what can the customer do during that time?
faqs.a: Think in three numbers: the film is held but soft for the first 24 hours, reaches most of its working strength by about 7 days, and fully cures (rated peel strength, all moisture flashed out) at around 30 days. No washing or heat for the first day, hand-wash only after a week, and no automatic washes or aggressive chemicals until full cure. A bubble still present at 30 days isn't water — it's contamination or an install defect.

faqs.q: Should I cut the film on the car or use pre-cut patterns?
faqs.a: Use plotter-cut patterns wherever possible — every blade cut on a panel is a chance to score the clear coat underneath, and that's a risk you're passing on to the customer. Confirm the pattern matches the exact year, model and trim before you start. If a cut on the vehicle is genuinely unavoidable, use a fresh blade every time, minimal pressure, cut on a fine-line tape stop rather than free-hand, and note the cut location in the job record.

faqs.q: What changes when I install matt PPF instead of gloss?
faqs.a: Matt is a different product, not just a different finish. Wear nitrile gloves and never touch the show side — matt holds fingerprints and skin oil far more visibly than gloss. Wrap your squeegee blade in a fresh microfibre or felt sleeve so you don't burnish the surface to gloss, use the lightest pressure that still moves the slip out, keep tack-solution alcohol low, and don't leave masking tape on the film any longer than the work needs (tape adhesive leaves a permanent gloss line). Keep more distance with the heat gun too — excess heat flattens the texture into shiny patches that won't heal back.

handoutRefs.title: Matt and Gloss PPF — Surfaces, GU Matching, and Install Differences

faqs.q: How clean does the bay actually need to be?
faqs.a: Clean enough that nothing lands under the film — inclusions are almost always airborne dust. Wet-mop or HEPA-vacuum before the day starts, keep doors closed and foot traffic down during prep and install, and blow down edges and panel gaps with compressed air right before the film goes on. Aim for a stable 18–24 °C bay at moderate humidity, with strong movable lighting so you can see specks before they're trapped. Film should go on within minutes of the final wipe, not hours.

faqs.q: There's haze and little bubbles under the film right after install. Is something wrong?
faqs.a: No — this is the most normal thing about a fresh install. The film is fitted with a water-and-soap slip solution, and a little moisture always stays behind and breathes out through the film as it cures. You'll see a slightly milky haze or small water pockets that shrink and clear on their own, usually within 7–14 days (faster in warm, dry, sunny weather). Don't press, poke or massage them. The golden rule for the first couple of weeks: look at the car, don't touch the film.

faqs.q: When can I first wash my car after PPF?
faqs.a: Leave it for at least the first 7 days, ideally 14, while the film cures. After that, hand wash only, and keep it out of automatic car washes permanently. Brush washes carry grit that scratches the film, and touchless ones rely on chemicals harsher than the film needs. Wash in the shade on a cool panel, top down to the dirtier lower panels, with a shampoo made for paint protection film and a soft microfibre mitt, and dry with a plush microfibre or a blower. If a bird dropping or bug lands during the first week, soak it and dab it off gently with clean water and a soft cloth — don't rub or use chemicals.

faqs.q: Can I use an automatic car wash or a pressure washer on PPF?
faqs.a: Avoid automatic washes, especially brush washes — the brushes carry grit and can scratch the film and dull matt finishes. A pressure washer is fine if used correctly: keep the nozzle 30–50 cm back, use a wide-fan tip (not a needle or zero-degree jet), keep it moving, and never aim straight at a film edge — pressure forced under an edge is the most common cause of avoidable lifting. Around badges, mirrors and lights, ease off or skip the pressure washer entirely.

sources.label: How to wash your car after PPF (32autostore)

faqs.q: What products are safe on PPF, and can I wax it?
faqs.a: Use a car shampoo made for paint protection film, with soft microfibre mitts. pH-neutral is not the test — it describes the acidity and says nothing about whether a product is safe on film, and a film-safe shampoo is not necessarily pH-neutral, so check the label says it is for PPF. Avoid abrasive polishes, cutting compounds, scouring pads and household cleaners, and avoid solvent-based products not rated for PPF. Traditional waxes with petroleum distillates (kerosene, naphtha) aren't recommended; if you want extra slickness and easier cleaning, a PPF-safe ceramic coating or a coating-compatible booster spray is the better route. On matt film, never use wax, clay or machine polish — they create permanent shiny patches. When in doubt, use the products your installer recommends.

handoutRefs.title: PPF Materials, Top Coats, and Ceramic Layers

faqs.q: I can see the edge of the film up close. Is that a fault?
faqs.a: Usually not. There are two fitting styles: pre-cut (plotter-cut), where the film stops a couple of millimetres short of the panel edge to keep the blade off your paint — that leaves a faint, normal edge line; and wrapped, where the film is taken around the edge so it's almost invisible, which costs more time and material. A fine, clean edge line is normal and expected. What isn't normal is an edge that's visibly peeling back, lifting, or letting dirt underneath — that's worth a call to your installer.

faqs.q: How long does PPF last?
faqs.a: A modern, well-installed and well-cared-for film typically performs for around 7–10 years, sometimes longer. End of life shows up gradually — slight yellowing, loss of self-healing, or edges starting to lift on older film — and at that point the film can usually be removed and replaced without harming the paint. Where the car lives matters: cars parked outdoors in strong sun age their film faster, because UV is the biggest long-term factor.

faqs.q: A stone went through the film and left a mark. Did the PPF fail?
faqs.a: No — that's the film doing exactly its job. PPF is a sacrificial layer: when a stone hits hard enough you may see a chip, dimple or even a small puncture in the film, but the paint underneath has been spared the damage it would otherwise have taken. A punctured panel of film can be replaced on its own while the rest of the installation keeps protecting the car. Remember PPF is Paint Protection Film, not Paint Perfection Film — it absorbs damage rather than preventing every mark.

faqs.q: A bubble or lifted edge appeared a couple of weeks after install. What should I do?
faqs.a: Don't pick at it, don't push it down with a fingernail, and don't try a household-glue repair — those cause more damage than the lift itself. Take a clear photo and contact your installer. Most edge lifts are quickly sorted with heat and proper technique on a return visit, and many installers build a free post-installation check-up into the job for exactly this. If something looks off and you're not sure, send a photo before doing anything.

faqs.q: The pre-cut kit doesn't quite fit this car. What do I do?
faqs.a: Modern templating software carries many trim versions for most cars, so a true pattern mismatch is rarer than it used to be — the real danger now is picking the wrong layout version. The options that change the pattern are the ones to watch: front and rear cameras, radar behind the badge or bumper, PDCs (parking sensors), carbon parts, and right- or left-hand drive (which changes the mirrors). Picking the right version depends on knowing the exact car, so have clear, self-explanatory photos of the actual vehicle, or the car itself, in front of you while you choose the trim options. Match the template to that car before you cut. There's no useful dry test on the car after that — the piece is plotter-cut on its backing sheet, which stays in one big piece with several parts often nested on it, so you can't lay it on the panel to check fit, and you never lay bare PPF adhesive down dry anyway (it grabs on contact and picks up dust, static and skin oils). Some form differences between the pattern and the car only come to light during the wet install itself, once the piece is peeled and floating on slip solution. So position it wet, check it against every edge as you go, and be ready to adapt: if it's short on one edge but good elsewhere, reposition while it floats to favour the visible edges and plan a wrapped or tucked edge where the shortfall lands. If the kit is simply wrong for the trim (wrong bumper, wrong mirror), stop and get the right pattern rather than forcing it — a stretched-to-fit piece pulls back later. Note any deviation from the standard kit in the job record.

faqs.q: How far should I tuck film into a panel gap?
faqs.a: Tuck far enough that the cut edge is hidden and the tension is anchored, usually 3–5 mm, but only where there's a real gap to take it. Use a plastic tuck tool, never metal, work the film in with the gap dry and the film warm, then post-heat so it stays. Don't force a tuck where the gap is too tight — a half-tucked edge that springs back looks worse than a clean trimmed edge. Where you can't tuck, a wrapped or relieved edge is the alternative.

faqs.q: If I have to trim on the paint, how do I avoid scoring the clear coat?
faqs.a: If you have to trim on the panel, first check whether you can cut over a barrier of tape between the film and the paint, so the blade rides on tape and the clear coat stays protected — lay fine-line knifeless tape or a strip of low-tack tape under the cut line, or pull knifeless cut-line tape through the film. Lean on that barrier until you have enough experience to score the PPF cleanly without cutting through to the paint. Either way, use a fresh snap-blade tip, the lightest pressure that parts the film, and a single confident pass rather than sawing. Free-hand blade cuts that reach the clear coat are the fastest way to leave a witness line you'll be paying to polish out.

faqs.q: Where should relief cuts go so they don't show?
faqs.a: Hide them in shut-lines, panel gaps and under trim where the eye doesn't travel, and keep them as short as the tension demands. A relief cut releases stretch the film can't absorb on a compound curve; placed in the open field it becomes a permanent visible seam and a dirt entry point. Plan the cut before you make it, post-heat the released edge, and never relief-cut just to save a minute of stretching.

faqs.q: How much gap should a pre-cut piece leave from the panel edge?
faqs.a: Around 2–3 mm on a pre-cut (plotter) install, with the cut line running along the light edge — on the flat just before the radius at the panel edge begins to curve away. That keeps the blade off the paint and gives a clean, near-invisible line. Less than that and the edge risks catching; more and the gap reads as a fault to the customer. If the customer wants no visible edge at all, that's a wrapped install: more time, more film, and a price to match. Set that expectation at quoting, not at handover.

faqs.q: How often should I change the blade?
faqs.a: Every piece, and the moment it drags. A blade is the cheapest thing on the bench and the most expensive thing to get wrong — a dull tip needs more pressure, and more pressure on the paint is how clear coats get scored. Snap or swap to a fresh edge before each cut on or near the car, and keep used blades in a sealed sharps tin, not loose in the bin.

faqs.q: When a panel needs two pieces, how should the join run?
faqs.a: It depends on the film. On clear PPF you avoid overlaps: an overlapped edge shows, so two pieces are split with a fine butt-join or a small gap on a natural line, or the panel is covered in one piece using wider film. Overlapping is a coloured-PPF (colour-change) technique, closer to vinyl wrap, where the colour hides the seam — there you shingle it so it sheds water and air: upper piece over lower, front over rear in the direction of travel, kept tight at 3–5 mm and post-heated down. On clear film, a visible overlap is a fault, not a finish.

faqs.q: Why is there a seam on my bonnet instead of one piece of film?
faqs.a: Film comes in roll widths, and a wide bonnet or roof can be wider than the roll, so it's covered in two pieces split along a natural line. On clear film that join is a fine butt-join or small gap, not an overlap, because an overlap would show — a neat split is normal and doesn't weaken the protection. Some shops offer seamless single-piece coverage on big panels using wider film at extra cost; if a seamless bonnet matters to you, ask about it before the job, not after.

faqs.q: Anything different about putting PPF on headlights?
faqs.a: Headlights are high-value and high-curve, so they reward patience. Clean and degrease the lens like paint, work the compound curve in small stretched sections, and tuck the edge into the gap between lens and bodywork so no edge sits in the airflow. Keep post-heat moderate — you're heating a plastic lens, not steel, so it warms faster and you don't want to distort it. Done right, the film takes the stone hits the lens would otherwise wear, and a clouded film panel is far cheaper to replace than a headlight.

handoutRefs.title: PPF Materials, Top Coats, and Ceramic Layers

faqs.q: Will PPF on my headlights make them go yellow?
faqs.a: Quality film with a UV-stable top coat shouldn't yellow the lens; if anything it shields the headlight's own plastic from the UV that makes factory lenses haze and yellow over the years. Low-grade film can discolour, which is one reason the film you choose matters. When the film eventually ages it's removed and replaced, and the lens underneath has been protected the whole time.

handoutRefs.title: PPF Materials, Top Coats, and Ceramic Layers

faqs.q: Can I put PPF on textured or matte plastic trim?
faqs.a: On smooth, painted or gloss plastic, yes — prep and install much as you would paint, but keep post-heat gentle because plastic warms and distorts faster than steel. Raw textured or grained plastic is a different story: the adhesive only touches the high points of the texture, so the bond is weak and edges lift early. Set the expectation honestly — textured trim is a poor PPF candidate, and a coating or a trim-specific product is often the better answer.

handoutRefs.title: PPF Materials, Top Coats, and Ceramic Layers

faqs.q: Can I install over fresh paint or a respray?
faqs.a: Not straight away. Fresh paint keeps off-gassing solvents for weeks, and sealing it under film can trap them and cause adhesion or bubbling problems. The common trade guidance is to let a respray cure for around 30 days — confirm the figure with the painter — before wrapping, and to make sure no fresh polish or sealant is on the panel. On factory OEM paint there's no wait; that's fully cured.

faqs.q: Which parts are most worth protecting if I'm not doing the whole car?
faqs.a: The parts that take the hits: a full front (bumper, bonnet, front of the wings, mirror backs, and usually the headlights), plus door edges and the door-handle cups where fingernails and rings wear the paint, and the rear loading lip if you load a boot a lot. That covers most real-world stone chips and daily wear for a fraction of a full-car price. Your installer can map a partial package to how and where you actually drive.

handoutRefs.title: Quoting — Building a Defensible Price for Every Job

faqs.q: Customers ask about PPF on wheels, sills and interior trim. Does it work?
faqs.a: PPF is designed for exterior painted and clear surfaces, and that's where it performs. It can be applied to some smooth interior piano-black trim to stop swirl marks, and to painted sills and rocker panels for chip protection, which are good uses. Wheels and brake calipers run hot and flex, so standard PPF isn't the right tool — point those customers at a coating or a heat-rated product instead. When a surface is outside what the film's made for, say so rather than taking the job and the comeback.

handoutRefs.title: PPF Materials, Top Coats, and Ceramic Layers

faqs.q: What's the right way to remove old PPF without damaging paint?
faqs.a: Heat and patience. Warm a corner to soften the adhesive, lift it with a fingernail or plastic tool (never metal), and peel slowly, keeping the heat moving just ahead of your peeling hand. Fold the film back on itself and pull it low and almost flat against the surface rather than straight up; that keeps the stress on the glue, not the clear coat. Steam or hot demineralised water works as well as a heat gun and is gentler on the paint. Pull too fast or too cold and the film tears into confetti, which turns a one-hour job into four. On sound factory paint this is safe; the risk is always the tool, the speed, and the angle, not the film itself.

faqs.q: The film left adhesive behind. How do I get it off?
faqs.a: Soften the residue with a dedicated automotive adhesive remover or isopropyl alcohol on a microfibre, let it dwell around 30 seconds, and wipe in straight lines until clean. Avoid acetone, lacquer thinner and razor blades — they strip clear coat. Older film and cheaper adhesives leave more residue, so budget extra time on a film that's been on for years. Finish with a panel wipe so the paint is clean before anything new goes on.

faqs.q: Old film is brittle and coming off in tiny shreds. Any faster way?
faqs.a: Not really — old, UV-baked film with degraded adhesive is the worst removal there is, and the only answer is more heat, more dwell, and working a small area at a time. A steam cleaner held 15–30 cm back adds heat and moisture and can help the shreds release in bigger pieces. Quote removal of aged film as its own line on the job, because it can take longer than the new install. This is also the argument for replacing film before it reaches end of life, not after.

faqs.q: If I take the PPF off, will it pull my paint off with it?
faqs.a: On sound factory paint, no — properly removed film comes off the clear coat cleanly, and the paint underneath is usually in better shape than the unprotected panels around it. The exception is paint that was already weak: an aftermarket respray, prior bodywork, or chips where the paint edge was already lifting. A good installer checks for those at intake and warns you before removal. Have it done professionally rather than attacking it with a hairdryer and a kitchen knife.

faqs.q: Can I replace just the bumper film that got chewed up, or does it all come off?
faqs.a: Single panels can be replaced on their own — that's one of the points of PPF. The damaged piece comes off, the panel is cleaned and re-prepped, and a new piece goes on, while the rest of the installation keeps protecting the car. Colour and gloss usually match fine when the same film is used, though film that's been weathering for years can look very slightly different next to a brand-new panel. For one chewed-up bumper, replacing that piece is the normal fix.

faqs.q: After stripping old film, what prep does the panel need before re-wrapping?
faqs.a: Treat it as a full prep, not a quick wipe. Once the film and all adhesive residue are off, wash, iron-decontaminate and clay the panel, then do the final degreaser wipe just as you would on a new car — the old adhesive and remover leave a film that wrecks the new bond if you skip it. Inspect for any clear-coat damage or chips that removal revealed and document them before you re-wrap. The new film is only as good as the prep under it.

faqs.q: How long after installing PPF can I apply a ceramic coating over it?
faqs.a: Let the film cure first so you don't seal in moisture or movement. A common working rule is to wait about 7 days before coating over fresh PPF, though it ranges from a day or two up to two weeks depending on the film and conditions — check the film maker's guidance. The film should be fully settled and free of haze and bubbles before you coat; coat too early and you can trap a bubble or lock in a moving edge. Decontaminate and panel-wipe the film surface first so the coating bonds to clean top coat.

handoutRefs.title: PPF Materials, Top Coats, and Ceramic Layers

faqs.q: I've got PPF — is there any point adding a ceramic coating on top?
faqs.a: They do different jobs, and many owners run both. PPF takes the physical hits (stones, scratches, abrasion); a ceramic coating on top makes the surface slicker and more water-repellent, so the film stays cleaner, resists staining and water spots, and washes more easily. It's optional, not essential — the film protects the paint either way — but coating the film is a sensible way to keep it looking fresh for longer. On matt film, only use a coating rated for matt.

handoutRefs.title: PPF Materials, Top Coats, and Ceramic Layers

faqs.q: If I coat over the PPF, do I still need to wash it carefully?
faqs.a: Yes. A coating makes washing easier, it doesn't make the car self-cleaning. You still hand wash with a shampoo made for paint protection film, still avoid harsh brushes and abrasive products, and still treat the film edges gently. The coating buys you slicker, less-frequent cleaning and better stain resistance, not a free pass. Bird droppings and bug splatter still need to come off promptly.

handoutRefs.title: PPF Materials, Top Coats, and Ceramic Layers

faqs.q: Does a ceramic coating stop PPF from self-healing?
faqs.a: A thin, film-rated ceramic coating sits on top and still lets the self-healing top coat warm and reflow, so light swirl marks heal as normal. The thing to avoid is a thick, glass-hard coating not designed for PPF — it can mask or stiffen the surface and interfere with healing, and it's far harder to remove later. Use a coating the film maker or coating maker rates for PPF, follow their cure window, and you keep the self-heal you sold the customer.

handoutRefs.title: PPF Materials, Top Coats, and Ceramic Layers

faqs.q: A customer has a coating already. Can I PPF over it?
faqs.a: PPF should go on bare, properly prepped paint, not on top of a ceramic coating — the adhesive is designed to bond to clear coat, and a coating in between weakens that bond and invites edge lift. If the car is already coated where you need to wrap, the coating has to come off those panels (machine decontamination or a light polish) so the film bonds to clean clear coat. The right order is paint, then PPF, then a coating on top if wanted.

handoutRefs.title: PPF Materials, Top Coats, and Ceramic Layers

faqs.q: Can I install PPF in winter, and what has to change?
faqs.a: You can, as long as the bay and the panel are warm enough — don't install below the film maker's minimum panel temperature, and aim for a stable 20–25 °C on the panel, not just in the air. Heat the bay ahead of time, warm your slip and tack solutions, and let a cold car come up to shop temperature before you start, because a cold panel kills tack and cold film is brittle and prone to stretch marks. The job takes longer in winter; plan for it rather than rushing a cold install that lifts in a fortnight.

faqs.q: Does cold weather cause condensation problems on the panel?
faqs.a: It can. A cold car brought into a warm, humid bay will sweat, and you can't bond film to a damp panel. Let the vehicle acclimatise, dry every panel and gap thoroughly, and do your final degreaser wipe once the surface is at shop temperature and dry. Keep humidity moderate and stable; a damp bay also keeps slip solution from flashing off, which slows the whole job.

faqs.q: Where should I store film and solutions in winter?
faqs.a: Indoors, at room temperature. Film stored cold goes stiff and is more likely to crease and stretch-mark when you handle it, and slip or tack solutions that have been near freezing won't behave predictably. Bring everything up to a steady 18–24 °C well before the job, and keep rolls flat or upright as the maker specifies so they don't take a set. Cold tools and cold hands slow you down too.

faqs.q: Do I need more post-heat when it's cold?
faqs.a: You need the same surface temperature — 80–90 °C measured at the film — but it's harder to reach and hold in a cold bay, and the film cools faster once you stop. Work in smaller sections, hold each heated edge down until it actually cools in position, and check with an IR thermometer rather than trusting the gun. Don't compensate by cranking the gun closer; that spikes the surface well past the ~100 °C ceiling and risks the film and clear coat. Warm bay, patient passes.

handoutRefs.title: SOP — Post-Heating: Surface Temperature and Technique

faqs.q: It's freezing out. Is it safe for the customer to drive off straight after a winter install?
faqs.a: The film is on, but the bond is still young — cold slows curing, so the first-24-hours rule matters even more in winter. Keep the car in the warm bay as long as the schedule allows so the adhesive gets a head start, then tell the customer to avoid car washes and to expect the curing haze to take longer to clear in cold, dark weather. Driving in the cold and wet is fine; pressure-washing a fresh edge in freezing weather is not.

handoutRefs.title: The Handover — Returning the Car the Right Way

faqs.q: Why do PPF quotes vary so much?
faqs.a: Price tracks coverage, the car, the film, and the installer. How much of the car you protect is the biggest lever (a partial front costs a fraction of a full body), followed by the size of the vehicle and how complex the panels are to wrap, the grade of film, and the prep and skill of the shop. A cheap quote usually means less coverage, lesser film, or less time on prep — the part you can't see, but the part that decides whether it lasts. Compare like for like: same coverage, same film, same edge finish.

handoutRefs.title: Quoting — Building a Defensible Price for Every Job

faqs.q: Is PPF actually worth the cost?
faqs.a: It depends on the car and how you use it. On a car you'll keep, drive on chip-heavy roads, or that holds its value, PPF protects paint that's expensive to repair and can help resale — the film takes the damage instead of the panel. On an old runabout you'll sell soon, a full wrap rarely pays back, and a partial front may be plenty. A good installer will tell you where the money is well spent and where it isn't, rather than selling you the biggest package.

handoutRefs.title: Quoting — Building a Defensible Price for Every Job

faqs.q: How long will my car be in the shop?
faqs.a: Plan on roughly one to two days for a full front, and three to seven days for a full-car wrap, depending on the vehicle and how many pieces it takes. That's installation time; the film then keeps curing after you collect it. Shops that quote a couple of hours for a full front are either doing a very small job or rushing the prep and post-heat that make it last. Ask for the expected collection day when you book.

handoutRefs.title: What PPF Costs and How to Choose an Installer
The Handover — Returning the Car the Right Way
Quoting — Building a Defensible Price for Every Job

faqs.q: Can it be done while I wait?
faqs.a: A small job like a few door edges or a single panel, sometimes. A full front or full wrap, no — proper prep, careful fitting and post-heating take time, and the film needs to be left undisturbed as it starts curing. Rushing any of those is exactly what causes edges to lift later. It's worth leaving the car so the work isn't fighting the clock.

handoutRefs.title: The Handover — Returning the Car the Right Way

faqs.q: One shop quoted half what another did. What's the catch?
faqs.a: Usually one of four things: less coverage than you think, a cheaper film that yellows or lasts fewer years, less prep and post-heat time, or a less experienced fitter. None of that shows on day one — it shows in year three when an edge lifts or the film hazes. Get every quote to spell out the exact panels, the film brand and its warranty, and whether edges are trimmed or wrapped, then compare. Cheapest and dearest can both be wrong; matched-up quotes tell you the real difference.

handoutRefs.title: Quoting — Building a Defensible Price for Every Job

faqs.q: Does the price include a warranty?
faqs.a: Reputable installs come with two things: the film maker's product warranty (typically covering yellowing, cracking and delamination for a set number of years) and the installer's workmanship guarantee on the fit. Ask what each one covers, for how long, and what voids it — washing too soon or third-party damage usually isn't covered. Get it in writing with the invoice, not as a verbal promise.

handoutRefs.title: Warranty and Guarantee — What You Promise, What the Law Promises
Warranty Claims — Handling the Customer While You Wait
Invoicing — From Job Done to Money in the Bank

faqs.q: Can I protect part of the car now and add more later?
faqs.a: Yes, and it's a sensible way to spread the cost — start with the highest-wear areas (full front, door edges, handle cups) and add panels later. The one thing to confirm is film matching: ask the shop to note exactly which film and finish they used so a later addition matches, since films age and product lines change. Staging the work doesn't reduce the protection on the panels you've already done.

handoutRefs.title: Quoting — Building a Defensible Price for Every Job

faqs.q: What would void my PPF warranty?
faqs.a: The common ones: washing or exposing it to harsh chemicals before it's cured, automatic brush washes, abrasive products and DIY repairs, damage from accidents or vandalism, and removing or working on the film yourself. Many installer guarantees also require you to attend the free post-install check (typically 2–4 weeks after fitting); skip that appointment and the workmanship guarantee can lapse. Normal stone chips and the film doing its sacrificial job are not faults and don't void anything. Read the specific terms you were given — film-maker product warranties and installer workmanship guarantees each list their own exclusions.

handoutRefs.title: Warranty and Guarantee — What You Promise, What the Law Promises
Warranty Claims — Handling the Customer While You Wait

faqs.q: My film is starting to look yellow. Is that a warranty claim?
faqs.a: Possibly. Modern film with a good top coat shouldn't yellow within its rated life, so premature yellowing is usually covered by the film maker's product warranty — that's one of the defects these warranties exist for. Take dated photos, note when it started, and contact your installer, who handles the claim with the manufacturer. Film that has simply reached the end of its years has aged, not failed, and that's a replacement rather than a claim.

handoutRefs.title: Warranty Claims — Handling the Customer While You Wait
Warranty and Guarantee — What You Promise, What the Law Promises

faqs.q: A customer's film failed inside the warranty. How do I handle the claim?
faqs.a: Separate the two warranties first: a product defect (yellowing, cracking, delamination, adhesive failure where prep was sound) goes to the film maker; a fitting issue (an edge that wasn't set, a contamination bubble) is your workmanship and you put it right. Document the fault with photos and the job record, deal with the customer's car promptly whatever the cause, and chase the manufacturer claim separately so the customer isn't caught in the middle. The relationship is worth more than winning the argument over who pays.

handoutRefs.title: Warranty Claims — Handling the Customer While You Wait
Warranty and Guarantee — What You Promise, What the Law Promises

faqs.q: How do I tell a film defect from customer damage or just wear?
faqs.a: Defects are uniform and unprompted — even yellowing across panels, cracking or delamination with no impact, adhesive letting go where the prep was sound. Damage is localised and has a cause: a stone strike, a scrape, a chemical etch, a wash-induced scratch. Wear is gradual and expected near end of life. Your intake photos and QC sheet are what let you tell these apart months later, which is exactly why you take them.

handoutRefs.title: Warranty Claims — Handling the Customer While You Wait

faqs.q: If someone keys my car or a stone cracks the film, does the warranty replace it?
faqs.a: No — product warranties cover the film failing on its own (yellowing, cracking, peeling), not damage from the outside world. A keying, a crash or a hard stone strike is exactly the damage the film is there to take, and replacing that panel's film is a normal paid job, not a claim. The upside is that it's the film you're replacing, not repainting the car. Some owners cover this through their motor insurance; ask your installer for a quote to re-do the affected panel.

handoutRefs.title: Warranty Claims — Handling the Customer While You Wait

faqs.q: I'm selling the car. Does the PPF warranty transfer to the new owner?
faqs.a: It depends on the terms. Some film-maker warranties are tied to the vehicle and transfer with a sale, some are tied to the original buyer and don't, and installer workmanship guarantees vary too. Check your paperwork and ask the installer before you sell — a transferable warranty and a documented install are a genuine selling point. Keep the invoice and warranty documents with the car's history file.

handoutRefs.title: Warranty and Guarantee — What You Promise, What the Law Promises

faqs.q: How is caring for matt PPF different from gloss?
faqs.a: The rules are stricter because you can't polish matt back to life. Never wax, polish, clay or use any product meant to add shine — they leave permanent glossy patches. Use only matt-rated shampoos and, if you coat it, a matt-rated coating; wash gently, and deal with bird droppings and bugs quickly before they etch. Treated kindly, matt film keeps its even, flat finish; treated like gloss, it gets shiny scars that can't be undone.

handoutRefs.title: Matt and Gloss PPF — Surfaces, GU Matching, and Install Differences

faqs.q: Can I put matt PPF over glossy paint to change the look?
faqs.a: Yes — matt film over gloss paint is a common way to give a car a satin look while protecting it, and it's reversible because the film comes off later to reveal the original gloss. Install it like any matt film: gloves on, fresh squeegee sleeve, light pressure, low tack-solution alcohol, and gentle heat so you don't burnish it shiny. Set the customer's expectation that the whole car needs consistent coverage for an even look, since matt film next to gloss paint is an obvious contrast.

handoutRefs.title: Matt and Gloss PPF — Surfaces, GU Matching, and Install Differences

faqs.q: A replacement matt panel looks a different flatness from the rest. Why?
faqs.a: Matt finish is measured in gloss units (GU), and not all matt films sit at the same level — mixing batches, products or finishes shows up as one panel looking flatter or shinier than its neighbour under good light. Match the film product and ideally the batch when replacing a panel, and check the GU level against the existing film before you commit. Burnishing during install also raises gloss locally, so a 'mismatch' can sometimes be your own squeegee pressure, not the film.

handoutRefs.title: Matt and Gloss PPF — Surfaces, GU Matching, and Install Differences

faqs.q: Does matt PPF self-heal like the gloss kind?
faqs.a: Many matt films do self-heal light marks with warmth, but heat heals by reflowing the top coat, and too much heat on matt can shift the finish toward gloss in that spot. So light swirls often recover on their own in the sun, but don't take a heat gun to matt film yourself chasing a scratch — you risk a shiny patch that won't go back. If a mark won't clear, ask your installer rather than experimenting.

handoutRefs.title: Matt and Gloss PPF — Surfaces, GU Matching, and Install Differences
PPF Materials, Top Coats, and Ceramic Layers

faqs.q: When will the film look its best?
faqs.a: Give it time to cure. The curing haze and any small water pockets clear as the moisture breathes out, usually within 7–14 days and faster in warm, dry, sunny weather. By about 30 days the film has fully cured and is at its clearest and strongest. If you collect the car on a cold, grey day and it looks slightly milky, that's normal and temporary — don't judge the finish on day one.

faqs.q: Up close the film has a faint texture, like fine orange peel. Is that a defect?
faqs.a: A very slight texture is normal in some films, especially thicker ones, and it settles and flattens as the film cures and warms in the sun. It's the top coat, not dirt or a bad install, and from normal viewing distance it disappears. What's not normal is a hard ridge, a trapped speck, or texture that's clearly a contamination bump — if you can feel a distinct lump, send your installer a photo.

handoutRefs.title: PPF Materials, Top Coats, and Ceramic Layers

faqs.q: Will people be able to tell my car has PPF on it?
faqs.a: On a clear gloss film, properly fitted, most people won't notice — you might catch a faint edge line up close where a pre-cut piece stops short of the panel edge, which is normal. Wrapped edges hide even that, at extra cost. Matt film obviously changes the look by design. A well-installed gloss film should look like nothing's there from a step back, just deeper, better-protected paint.

faqs.q: Should I correct the paint before wrapping?
faqs.a: Do the correction the customer is paying for, but understand that clear film magnifies what's under it — swirls, sanding marks and dust nibs all show through and can't be fixed without removing the film. Agree the level of correction at quoting: a quick gloss-up, a one-step enhancement, or full multi-stage correction, and document the paint's condition at intake so there's no dispute later. Never machine-polish straight before wrapping without a fresh degrease afterward; polish oils and compound dust are exactly what stop the film bonding.

faqs.q: I've got a few chips and swirls already. Will PPF hide them?
faqs.a: Chips, no — those stay visible under clear film. Swirls are the awkward case: the film often does mask them, and that is a warning sign rather than a bonus, because it means the panel was filmed without being polished. At least a one-step machine polish belongs to preparing the surface — claying lifts bonded contamination but lightly marrs the paint, and the polish takes that marring back out — and the adhesive bonds better to corrected paint than to a marred one. A good installer will insist on it and quote it separately. Photograph any existing damage at intake so everyone agrees what was there.

faqs.q: I left a bird dropping on the film for a day. Is it ruined?
faqs.a: Probably fine, but get it off now. Bird droppings are acidic and, left baking in the sun, can etch even the film's top coat over time — the film takes that hit instead of your paint, which is the point, but a fresh dropping wipes off easily and a baked-on one doesn't. Soak it with water or a PPF-safe cleaner, let it soften, and lift it gently rather than scrubbing it dry. If a dull mark stays after cleaning, the self-healing top coat may lift it with warmth, so give it some sun before worrying.

handoutRefs.title: PPF Materials, Top Coats, and Ceramic Layers

faqs.q: How do I get tar or tree sap off PPF?
faqs.a: Promptly and gently. Use a PPF-safe tar-and-sap remover or a little isopropyl alcohol on a soft cloth, let it dwell to soften the deposit, then wipe it away — don't pick or scrape at it. Avoid strong solvents, petrol or anything not rated for film, since they can dull or stain the top coat. The longer tar or sap sits, especially in the sun, the harder it bonds, so deal with it the day you spot it.

faqs.q: Does winter road salt damage PPF?
faqs.a: Salt won't eat the film the way it attacks bare metal, which is one reason a protected front end is handy in winter. The thing to watch is salt and grit collecting along film edges and in panel gaps, where it holds moisture and grime — rinse the car more often in winter, pay attention to the edges, and don't blast a pressure washer straight at them. A film edge kept clean is a film edge that stays down.

faqs.q: I'm getting water spots on the film. How do I deal with them?
faqs.a: Water spots are mineral deposits left when hard water dries on the surface, not damage to the film. Dry the car after washing rather than letting it air-dry, wash in the shade so it doesn't flash-dry, and for spots that have already formed use a PPF-safe water-spot remover. A ceramic coating over the film helps here, because the slicker surface lets water bead and run off instead of sitting and drying.

handoutRefs.title: PPF Materials, Top Coats, and Ceramic Layers

faqs.q: Petrol splashed on the film at the pump. Will it stain?
faqs.a: A quick splash that you wipe off is nothing to worry about — modern film top coats shrug off the occasional fuel contact. What you don't want is fuel left to sit and dry, which can dull or stain the surface over time. Rinse or wipe the area with water and a soft cloth when you get home. A filler-flap area that catches drips regularly is exactly the kind of high-contact spot PPF is good at protecting.

faqs.q: Can I scrape ice off a panel that has PPF?
faqs.a: Don't use a metal or hard plastic ice scraper on film — it can gouge the surface or lift an edge. Clear ice with a de-icer spray, lukewarm (never boiling) water, or a soft brush, and let it melt rather than chipping at it. Brushing snow off with a soft snow brush is fine. As with washing, the edges are the vulnerable part, so keep scrapers and hard tools away from them.

faqs.q: What does 'self-healing' actually mean?
faqs.a: The film's outer top coat is an elastic polymer that softens slightly with heat and flows back to flat, so light swirl marks and fine scratches that only touch the top coat disappear when the panel warms up — a sunny day, a warm wash, or gentle heat from a hair dryer. It heals surface marring, not deep cuts that go through the top coat, and not stone punctures. It's a real, repeatable property of good film, not a one-time trick.

handoutRefs.title: PPF Materials, Top Coats, and Ceramic Layers

faqs.q: What's the difference between TPU and TPH film, and does it matter?
faqs.a: It matters a lot for how long the job lasts. TPU (thermoplastic polyurethane) is the premium material — strong, elastic, optically clear, with proper heat-activated self-healing — and it typically lasts the full 7–10 years without yellowing. TPH (a cheaper hybrid) is stiffer, harder to stretch, self-heals poorly if at all, and tends to yellow and reach end of life sooner, often in 3–5 years. A cheap quote is often a TPH film; if you're comparing prices, this is usually the difference you can't see on day one.

handoutRefs.title: PPF Materials, Top Coats, and Ceramic Layers

sources.label: TPU vs TPH vs PVC PPF (Teckwrap)

faqs.q: How thick is PPF — will it look like a layer stuck on?
faqs.a: A typical film is around 150–200 microns total (roughly 6–8 thousandths of an inch): a tough polyurethane layer, the adhesive, and the self-healing top coat. That's thick enough to absorb stone strikes but thin enough that, fitted well with neat edges, it looks like part of the paint rather than a layer on top. The thickness is doing the work — it's what lets the film take a hit your paint would otherwise feel.

handoutRefs.title: PPF Materials, Top Coats, and Ceramic Layers

faqs.q: Does PPF only come in clear gloss?
faqs.a: No. The common one is clear gloss, which protects while keeping your paint's original look. Matt (satin) film protects and turns a glossy car to a flat finish, and it's reversible when removed. There are also coloured and 'stealth' films that change the colour or finish entirely while protecting underneath. They're all PPF; the finish is your choice, though matt and coloured films have their own care rules.

handoutRefs.title: PPF Materials, Top Coats, and Ceramic Layers
Matt and Gloss PPF — Surfaces, GU Matching, and Install Differences

faqs.q: Does the self-healing stop working after a while?
faqs.a: It fades gradually rather than switching off. As the top coat ages over years of UV and washing, it heals more slowly and less completely, and losing that self-healing is one of the signs a film is reaching end of life. On a quality TPU film that's typically well into the 7–10 year range; on a cheap film it can go much sooner. When healing stops and edges start to age, that's the cue to replace the film.

handoutRefs.title: PPF Materials, Top Coats, and Ceramic Layers

faqs.q: A customer wants the cheapest film. How should I advise them?
faqs.a: Be straight about what the price buys. A budget TPH film will protect for a few years but is more likely to yellow, won't self-heal well, and is harder to remove cleanly later; a TPU film costs more and lasts the distance. Frame it as years-per-euro, not sticker price, and let them choose with the facts — some genuinely want three years on a lease car, and that's a fair call. What you don't do is fit a cheap film and let them believe it's a premium one.

handoutRefs.title: PPF Materials, Top Coats, and Ceramic Layers
Quoting — Building a Defensible Price for Every Job

sources.label: TPU vs TPH vs PVC PPF (Teckwrap)

faqs.q: Can PPF go on a boat?
faqs.a: Yes, and it's a real use — film protects gelcoat and hull graphics from dock rash, UV chalking and abrasion, and there are marine-oriented films for it. Prep follows the same principle as a car: the surface must be clean, dry and degreased, and gelcoat that's already oxidised needs correcting first or the film bonds to a failing surface. Curves and large flat hull sections need the same stretch-and-set discipline as a bumper. It's slower work than a car, so price it accordingly.

handoutRefs.title: PPF Materials, Top Coats, and Ceramic Layers

faqs.q: Customers ask about PPF on furniture and worktops. Does it work?
faqs.a: It can — clear film protects high-wear surfaces like tabletops, desk edges and cabinet faces from scratches and scuffs, and the install principles carry straight over: clean, degrease, fit, set the edges. The surface needs to be smooth and sound; raw wood, textured laminate and anything flexing or oily is a poor candidate. It's a niche job, but the skills are the same ones you use on a car.

handoutRefs.title: PPF Materials, Top Coats, and Ceramic Layers

faqs.q: Is it safe to put PPF over my parking sensors and cameras?
faqs.a: Quality film is thin, and a careful installer trims around or neatly over sensors so nothing is left half-covered, but the safe rule is to follow your car maker's guidance — some makers (Tesla and Toyota among them) say not to film radar or ultrasonic sensor faces, because added thickness can affect how they read. Camera lenses and radar covers are usually left clear. A good installer knows which zones to leave alone on your model; if in doubt, ask before the job.

faqs.q: Will clear PPF change the colour of my paint?
faqs.a: A good clear gloss film is optically clear, so it shouldn't change the colour — if anything it can make the paint look a touch deeper and glossier. It won't darken or tint the car. Cheaper films can carry a faint cast or haze, and any film will yellow eventually if it's low quality or very old, which is another reason the film grade matters. On a quality film, fresh, you shouldn't be able to tell the colour changed at all.

handoutRefs.title: PPF Materials, Top Coats, and Ceramic Layers

faqs.q: Can the film itself be polished if it gets dull or scratched?
faqs.a: Light marring usually doesn't need polishing at all — the self-healing top coat lifts it with warmth. For dullness or fine marks that won't heal, the film can be lightly polished with a product rated for PPF, but aggressive compounds and cutting pads will damage the top coat, so it's a job for someone who knows film, not the same as correcting paint. On matt film, don't polish at all — it creates permanent shiny patches. When in doubt, ask your installer.

handoutRefs.title: PPF Materials, Top Coats, and Ceramic Layers

faqs.q: How do I pick a good PPF installer?
faqs.a: Look for clean, finished work you can inspect in person — tidy edges, no trapped dust, no lifting on cars they did months ago — and ask three questions: which film brand and grade they fit, what the warranty covers, and whether they work in a clean, temperature-controlled bay. A proper installer will happily talk prep and post-heat rather than just quoting a price. Cheapest rarely means best with PPF; the skill and the conditions are most of what you're paying for.

handoutRefs.title: Quoting — Building a Defensible Price for Every Job

faqs.q: Should I take the PPF off before I sell the car?
faqs.a: Usually leave it on — well-kept film is a selling point, it's protected the paint underneath, and a documented, possibly transferable warranty adds value. Take it off only if it's old and failing, or if a buyer specifically wants it gone, and have that done professionally so the paint isn't damaged on the way out. Either way, keep the install paperwork; proof the car's been protected helps at resale.

handoutRefs.title: Invoicing — From Job Done to Money in the Bank

faqs.q: Can someone install PPF at my home, or does it need a shop?
faqs.a: PPF really wants a clean, enclosed, temperature-controlled space — dust and bugs landing under the film during a driveway install are exactly what cause inclusions, and cold or wind ruin the bond. Some installers offer mobile work, but for anything more than a tiny job a proper bay gives a far more reliable result. If a job has to be done on site, it needs an enclosed, clean area at the right temperature, not an open driveway.

handoutRefs.title: The Handover — Returning the Car the Right Way

faqs.q: Do I have to do anything to keep the warranty valid?
faqs.a: Mostly just care for it as advised: wash with products made for paint protection film, avoid harsh chemicals and brush washes, deal with contaminants promptly, and don't attempt DIY repairs or removal. Some installers offer or recommend a periodic check-up; keeping that, and keeping your paperwork, makes any future claim straightforward. Neglect and obvious misuse are what put a warranty at risk, not normal driving.

handoutRefs.title: Warranty Claims — Handling the Customer While You Wait

faqs.q: What should I keep on file for each job in case of a future claim?
faqs.a: Enough to reconstruct the job months or years later: dated intake photos showing the paint's condition, the film brand, batch and which panels were wrapped, the QC sign-off, and a copy of the warranty terms the customer was given. If a claim or dispute comes up, that record is what separates a film defect from later damage and keeps you out of an argument you can't otherwise win. It's five minutes per job that saves hours later.

handoutRefs.title: Warranty Claims — Handling the Customer While You Wait
